item.title: Earth from Space: Typhoon Surigae
item.summary: Image: This false-colour, polarised image from Copernicus Sentinel-1 shows us the surface of the sea beneath the clouds, as seen by the satellite’s radar instrument. The sea conditions reflect the strong winds as Typhoon Surigae passes over.
item.page_text:
You have already liked this page, you can only like it once!
We are used to seeing satellite images of tropical storms from above the clouds, featuring the characteristic white swirls around the eye of the storm. This false-colour, polarised image from Copernicus Sentinel-1 shows us the surface of the sea beneath the clouds, as seen by the satellite’s radar instrument. The sea conditions reflect the strong winds as Typhoon Surigae passes over.
Zoom in to explore this image at its full resolution.
The image, captured on 28 September 2026, shows Typhoon Surigae as it was moving north-eastwards in an area of the Philippine Sea about 200 km south of the island of Shikoku, Japan. By 1 October, the storm, also known as Typhoon no. 26, was almost 1000 km away, roughly 200 km south of Tokyo. It is one of several typhoons in the Pacific Ocean at the moment.
The relatively calm seas at the eye of the storm are clearly visible in dark blue in this image. The colorful effect is created using two radar polarisations, each assigned to a different colour. The orange-yellow ring in the image is where the radar instrument has detected rough ocean conditions and strong winds.
The lighter blue areas of the image show where the radar has detected a different kind of signal and it most likely denotes ocean and wind conditions that differ to the bright yellow and orange areas. Some of the possible causes are lower wind speeds, less sea surface movement or areas of rain.
Some bright yellow flecks are seen in the lower part of the image. While these look like small islands, there are no land masses in that region – they are most likely to be areas of concentrated wind and rain.
When this radar image was acquired, Typhoon Surigae had strong winds with maximum gusts of up to 240 km per hour, with dangerous ocean conditions including strong swells and waves reaching up to 7 m. Since then, it has weakened considerably and is currently classed as a tropical depression, with maximum wind speeds of 55 km per hour.

item.title: Image of the week: Fires continue in southern Borneo
item.summary: Image of the week: Fires continue in southern Borneo Sarah Leach Fri, 02/10/2026 - 10:15 Image of the week: Fires continue in southern Borneo Watching our Earth from space This week’s image is a view of smoke plumes and haze from multiple fires in southern Kalimantan on the island of Borneo, Southeast Asia. The image was captured on 23 September 2026 by one of the Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellites. Last Updated Published on The smoke and haze are caused by a mix of agricultural burning and peatland fires, which have been exacerbated by El Niño -related drought conditions. The haze has caused severe air quality problems for millions of people living in affected parts of Southeast Asia. The fires are also affecting natural habitats and species, including the critically endangered Bornean orangutan. Fires image The main image was captured by the OLCI instrument onboard one of the Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellites on 23 September 2026. EUMETSAT operates the Sentinel-3 satellites, in cooperation with ESA, and delivers the marine and atmospheric data on behalf of the European Union. item.title: A Year of Lightning
item.summary: This animated map shows a year's worth of lightning strikes across the United States. The animation reveals the clear seasonal patterns of lightning storms across the U.S. As you watch the animation, you can see the country's lightning season move northwards with the changing seasons. During winter, lightning is largely confined to the Gulf Coast before activity spreads north in spring. By summer, thunderstorms are lighting up much of the country, with particularly intense activity across Florida and the Southwest, before the storms retreat south again in autumn. The map is one of the latest visualizations from the ever impressive mapped.earth . item.title: Providing Global Relief
item.summary: Bert Spaan has taken Mapterhorn's global terrain data to create an interactive global Relief map. What is particularly interesting about this new map is that, unlike traditional topographic maps with a fixed colour-to-elevation scale, the map's colour spectrum adapts dynamically to the specific region or bounds currently in view. As you pan and zoom across different landscapes, the colour grading shifts to highlight local topographic variations, producing a striking and constantly changing view of the world's mountains, valleys and plains. This works particularly well when switching between very different environments: the colour range changes to bring out the relief at the scale you're viewing, rather than leaving low-lying terrain looking uniformly flat. A number of controls allow you to adjust how the elevation data is visualized. You can switch between absolute and visible elevation ranges, lock the current colour range, reverse the colours, animate the colours, and cycle through different ways of handling elevation outliers. item.title: Drone LiDAR reveals previously unknown Aboriginal rock shelters in the Blue Mountains
item.summary: Archaeologists have used drone-mounted LiDAR technology to identify previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters containing rock art and stone ...
item.page_text:
The research was conducted by the Vere Gordon Childe Centre at the University of Sydney and the Australian Museum, working in partnership with the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation (DCAC).
Researchers deployed drones equipped with LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) to survey rugged areas of the Blue Mountains, where dense vegetation and difficult terrain have historically made conventional archaeological surveys challenging.
LiDAR works by emitting laser pulses and measuring their return to generate highly detailed three-dimensional models of the landscape. This enables researchers to identify topographical features that may otherwise be obscured by vegetation.
The drone surveys successfully confirmed the locations of six previously registered rock shelters and identified three unregistered shelters containing Aboriginal cultural material. Among the discoveries were stone artefacts and examples of rock art, including red hand stencils.
The surveys also produced more accurate geographical coordinates for known sites than those recorded in the Aboriginal Heritage Information Management System (AHIMS), the official register of Aboriginal places and objects in New South Wales.
Potential shelters identified from the aerial data were subsequently investigated on the ground by teams led by Dr Amy Mosig Way, a research archaeologist at the University of Sydney and the Australian Museum.
Wayne Brennan and Erin Wilkins of the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation then led the recording of rock art at confirmed cultural sites.
The research forms part of the Gulamada Project, which combines archaeological methods and emerging technologies with First Nations cultural knowledge to identify, document and protect Aboriginal heritage.
“From the outset, our vision for the Gulamada Project has been to create a true nexus of science and culture. This work highlights the importance of listening, learning and working together,” said Brennan, project co-director and an Indigenous rock art specialist at the University of Sydney.
More than 200 rock shelters containing archaeological and cultural evidence have already been documented across the Blue Mountains. However, researchers estimate that only around 10 per cent of the region has been systematically surveyed because of the area’s rugged landscape.
According to Dr Jacob Bongers, lead author of the study and a digital archaeologist at the University of Sydney, drone-based LiDAR could dramatically improve the efficiency of archaeological surveys in such environments.
“This work is exciting because it offers an efficient and accurate way to locate sites in rugged environments, which are notoriously arduous, expensive and time-consuming to survey,” said Bongers.
“Importantly, our methodology is helping expand the record of Aboriginal cultural sites in the Blue Mountains and has the potential to be applied in other regions.”
Beyond archaeological discovery, researchers say the technology could provide Aboriginal communities and heritage managers with another means of identifying cultural sites threatened by development, erosion, bushfires and other environmental pressures.
The team now plans to test and adapt the methodology in other Australian environments in partnership with Aboriginal communities, including the tropical savannahs of western Arnhem Land and the semi-arid landscapes of western New South Wales.
The study, “LiDAR-assisted survey locates unregistered rock shelters in the Blue Mountains, Australia”, is published in the journal Remote Sensing. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18203495

item.title: NASA satellites observe historic 2026 El Niño - Phys.org
item.summary: Credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio. One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water ...
item.page_text:
edited by Gaby Clark , 																								reviewed by Robert Egan
This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted
														the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:
A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely.
El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years, marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific.
As of October, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has said that there's an 83% chance that the strongest El Niño since 1950 is currently unfolding. People around the world, including farmers, firefighters and coastal communities, are already experiencing the effects in different ways.
Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.
One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water called a Kelvin wave was spotted near Micronesia in the western Pacific. Kelvin waves are slow-moving pulses of water thousands of miles long. Like underwater freeways, they transfer heat from west to east across the Pacific.
The warm water heats the air directly above it, making it rise. The change in air pressures weakens or even reverses the trade winds that typically blow in the opposing direction, from the Americas toward Asia, causing sea levels in the eastern Pacific to rise further and waters to warm even more. This chain reaction signifies the start of an El Niño.
The map above shows that by early April, those Kelvin waves had reached the eastern Pacific, and sea surface temperatures had begun to warm. Warm water expands in volume, elevating local sea levels in some areas by as much as 1 to 1.3 feet (30 to 40 centimeters). The higher-than-normal water can be seen sloshing toward South America then moving up the coast to California. Sea levels that are 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 centimeters) lower than normal are visible around Indonesia and northern Australia.
"Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Niño," said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "And our sea level satellites let us peer into the ocean and watch every beat."
Scientists have used satellite altimetry to track the height of the ocean with ultraprecision since 1993. That unbroken data record continues today with the Sentinel-6 satellites. State-of-the-art radar altimeters aboard these satellites survey millions of square miles of ocean in a single day, complementing NOAA's fleet of ocean sensors and buoys drifting and diving through the water below.
Warmer-than-normal seawater is one of the best-known indicators of El Niño. Already, sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific are about 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 degrees Celsius) warmer than the long-term average and could jump another fraction of a degree in the coming months, Willis said.
Satellites carrying microwave and infrared radiometers can see through and around clouds to measure heat energy at the sea surface. Satellites in 2026 mapped the band of warmer-than-normal water as it expanded throughout the spring. The band, seen in dark red, stretches for millions of square miles from the heart of the Pacific to the coast of South America.
Ocean temperatures can influence weather patterns around the world. Air above the water's surface carries heat and moisture into the atmosphere, seeding rainstorms and rearranging weather patterns across the globe.
Discover the latest in science, tech, and space with over 100,000 subscribers who rely on Phys.org for daily insights.
        Sign up for our free newsletter and get updates on breakthroughs,
        innovations, and research that matter— daily or weekly .
El Niño's warm waters also change the color of the ocean. A NASA satellite is tracking these subtle shifts in hues, as equatorial Pacific waters have become measurably bluer over the last several months.
"Some people think of water as being just blue, but it's amazing the multitude of colors the ocean can be," said Matthew Kehrli, a lead research scientist for the PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite team at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
This spectrum is in part thanks to microscopic plants called phytoplankton, which form the basis of the marine food web. There are thousands of different species of phytoplankton, which come in shades like teal, brown or green. This year, in areas of the Pacific Ocean along the equator that are typically lush with phytoplankton and greener as a result, these hues are waning.
This is an expected effect of El Niño. Phytoplankton thrive in cool, nutrient-rich waters, but during an El Niño, the weakening trade winds reduce the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface. With limited food supply, phytoplankton abundance drops. This decline can trigger cascading effects across the marine food web, forcing other marine life to relocate to new feeding grounds.
This year's El Niño is the first since PACE launched in 2024, providing new views of the phenomenon. The Ocean Color Instrument aboard PACE observes the ocean in hyperspectral color—across several hundred different wavelengths of visible, near-infrared and ultraviolet light—monitoring phytoplankton and other ocean-color changes in near-real time. With PACE data, researchers calculate the average color of the ocean, simplifying spectra of light into a single number, known as apparent visible wavelength.

item.title: The El Niño Forcast Map
item.summary: Much has been written about how this year's El Niño is already breaking records. Climate Dashboard's new interactive map lets you explore how this unusually strong El Niño could affect climate conditions around the world, including what it might mean for the weather where you live. El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which unusually warm ocean temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific disrupt atmospheric circulation, shifting rainfall and temperature patterns around the world. These effects can mean wetter conditions in some regions and drought in others. The El Niño Impacts layer in the Climate Dashboard provides a way to explore what this year's unusually strong El Niño could actually mean around the world. The map shows the predicted rainfall effects for each three-month season, from the current October-December forecast through to seasons ending in May 2027. Climate Dashboard's new interactive map lets you explore how this unusually strong El Niño could affect climate conditions around the world, including what it might mean for the weather where you live. El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which unusually warm ocean temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific disrupt atmospheric circulation, shifting rainfall and temperature patterns around the world. These effects can mean wetter conditions in some regions and drought in others. item.title: The Satellites of Mars
item.summary: There are lots of 3D maps that visualize the tens of thousands of human-made satellites orbiting the Earth, such as SatelliteeXplorer and James Darpinian's See a Satellite Tonight , which uses Google's Street View imagery to show you exactly where to look in the night sky if you want to watch a satellite passing overhead. Perigee takes a rather broader view of humanity's presence in space. As well as visualizing thousands of satellites orbiting the Earth, this impressive 3D viewer lets you explore spacecraft orbiting the Moon and Mars, and even track probes travelling through the wider Solar System. On Earth you can explore around 16,600 active catalogued satellites, with the option to filter them by operator, country, constellation, orbit type or launch site. You can also search for individual satellites by name or NORAD number and click on them to see details such as their operator, launch date and orbit. The same 3D interface can then be used to explore our planetary neighbours. item.title: Using AI to Annotate Vintage Maps
item.summary: Bosphore 1819 is an interactive version of a beautiful 1819 topographical map of the Bosphorus. The original Plan Topographique du Bosphore de Thrace ou Canal de Constantinople et de ses environs was surveyed by François Kauffer between 1776 and 1786, before being redrawn and expanded by Jean-Denis Barbié du Bocage and published in 1819. The original map is wonderfully detailed, but navigating it isn't particularly easy - particularly if you can't speak or read French. Hundreds of villages, palaces, fortifications, streams, capes and other landmarks are labelled using French spellings of Ottoman Turkish names. item.title: EarthCARE’s view of volcanic plume boosts air safety
item.summary: When Anak Krakatau erupted a few weeks ago, the European Space Agency’s EarthCARE satellite, orbiting above, captured vertical profiles of different constituents within the volcanic plume. Designed primarily to advance our understanding of how clouds and aerosols influence Earth’s climate, here EarthCARE also provided valuable information to support safe air travel. At the same time, these observations offer new insights into the impact that volcanic eruptions have on the climate system.
item.page_text:
When Anak Krakatau erupted a few weeks ago, the European Space Agency’s EarthCARE satellite, orbiting above, captured vertical profiles of different constituents within the volcanic plume. Designed primarily to advance our understanding of how clouds and aerosols influence Earth’s climate, here EarthCARE also provided valuable information to support safe air travel.
At the same time, these observations offer new insights into the impact that volcanic eruptions have on the climate system.
Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been active sporadically since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of the last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
While Anak Krakatau did not explode with the terrifying power of Krakatoa, which caused a devastating tsunami, today even relatively minor volcanic eruptions can have a major impact on air travel.
Located in the Sunda Strait between Sumatra and Java in Indonesia, Anak Krakatau started erupting on 4 September, leading to thousands of flights being grounded and hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded.
Volcanic ash can damage or even cause aircraft engines to stall, while also reducing pilots’ visibility by scratching cockpit windows. Toxic gases, such as sulphur dioxide, can further contaminate the cabin air supply. To mitigate these risks, a global network of nine Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres (VAAC) is responsible for providing aviation advice, each with the responsibility for a specific part of the globe.
The Anak Krakatau eruption came under the remit of the Darwin VAAC, operated by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), who were quick to add EarthCARE’s unique atmospheric lidar ( ATLID ) data to their suite of satellite monitoring tools.
Along with the cloud profiling radar (CPR), the multispectral imager (MSI) and the broadband radiometer (BBR), ATLID is one of EarthCARE’s four instruments – which are all used in in synergy to measure clouds and aerosols to deepen our understanding of how they regulate Earth’s energy balance.
ATLID is a highly specialised laser instrument. It sends pulses of ultraviolet light towards Earth and measures the light that scatters back to the satellite, providing a unique view of the tops of clouds and vertical profiles of atmospheric aerosols.
Not only does ATLID yield important information about the altitude and concentration of aerosols, but it can also be used with advanced algorithms to estimate types of aerosol – such as ash, smoke, sulphate, sea salt and desert dust.
The image below uses a capture from Copernicus Sentinel-3 on 5 September overlaid with data from EarthCARE’s MSI, ATLID and CPR instruments. The image also notes aircraft flight levels: most aircraft cruise around FL350, which means 35,000 ft (about 10,700 m).
The swath from the MSI instrument shows the volcanic plume in false colour, with purple areas highlighting ash, and bright green indicating sulphur dioxide gas.
Above the MSI swath, the vertical curtain shows a range of different types of aerosols measured by ATLID and by the CPR. These aerosol types are spread in layers of optically thin and thick sulphate, fine ash, and a distinct feature of what is thought to be coarse ash (dark brown).
The area shaded in grey is a region where ATLID’s laser beam cannot penetrate through the optically thick layer of sulphate particles (orange) above, and where CPR lacks sensitivity to fine ash.
Robin Hogan, from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), explained, “The CPR has a very different sensitivity to atmospheric particles than ATLID: its much longer wavelength means that it is much more sensitive to large particles and much less sensitive to small particles. Normally we would expect the particles in a volcanic plume 200 km from the source to be too small to be detected by a radar.
“However, thanks to the unprecedentedly high sensitivity of the CPR, it detects a feature extending from the surface up to around 6 km (dark brown), which is believed to correspond to larger ash aggregates that are settling out of the plume.”
Helen Dacre, from the University of Reading in the UK, added, “If confirmed, this would provide useful evidence that large ash particles can remain aloft for longer, and travel farther, than is often assumed. The observation, therefore, offers a valuable opportunity to constrain both ash sedimentation rates and long-range transport processes in volcanic ash dispersion models.”
While there remains speculation as to what’s actually in the grey area and this requires further study – the message is simple to the aviation authorities: do not fly aircraft here.
Andy Prata of BOM said, “Together with the VAAC forecasters, we were able to verify the forecast guidance of the westward moving plume at FL500, which is at the altitude of around 15 km. ATLID was crucial to help forecasters verify the altitude of the upper-level component of the plume.”
Shannon Mason also from ECWMF said, “The separate, layered and interacting plumes of ash, clouds, gases and aerosols from volcanic eruptions are complex and evolve rapidly.
“With a timely observation from EarthCARE we were able to grasp the vertical structure of this event in near-real time to inform aviation advice – and scientists will continue using EarthCARE’s measurements to better understand how ash and other volcanic aerosols behave in the hours and days after an eruption.”
ESA’s Alex Hoffmann added, “While immediately challenging for aviation, the impacts of major volcanic eruptions can be much longer lasting. Sulphate aerosols injected into the stratosphere by the 1883 Krakatoa eruption persisted for more than a year, reflecting incoming sunlight and causing temporary global cooling.
“Understanding the injection altitude of volcanic material and its optical properties is particularly important to understand climate impacts – information that EarthCARE's lidar is well positioned to provide.”
